correctness.rationale: The known Fibonacci ν2 formula gives s(n)=h(ν2(n+1)) when 6 divides n+1 and 0 otherwise, h(t)=floor((t+2)/2). Define g(n)=δ2(n)h(ν2(n+1)) with δj indicating n mod3. For each e>=1 and i<4^e−1, s(4^e n+i) is zero for odd i+1 or equals h(ν2(i+1)) δ_{−i−1 mod3}(n) for even i+1; the final offset gives g+eδ2. Thus all kernel sequences lie in span(s,g,δ0,δ1,δ2). The explicit subsequences s(16n+1)=δ1, s(16n+5)=δ0, s(64n+9)=δ2 and s(4n+3)=g+δ2 show each generator lies in the kernel module. At n=0,1,2,5,11 the resulting 5x5 witness matrix has determinant ±1; hence rank exactly five. All kernel depths are covered symbolically.

originality.rationale: Murru–Sanna explicitly leave the rank of ν_k(u_(n+1)) for composite k, including prime powers, open. Their rank-five prime-base Fibonacci valuation is NOT this statement: changing both ν2 to floor(ν2/2) and the 2-kernel to the 4-kernel changes the generated rational module. The five-generator computation answers a natural specific composite-base question not provided by inspected prior theorems.
